full_texts.title: Central Bank Opens Bitcoin and Ethereum to Retail Investors This Month. Can a 300,000 Local Currency Cap Move the BTC and ETH Price?
full_texts.text:
The country just handed ordinary citizens a legal path to Bitcoin and Ethereum, yet a major trading partner and a regional rival shrugged. Between sanctions, broker bottlenecks, and heavy ETF outflows in the US, one number may matter far less than headlines suggest.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
The central bank opened the crypto market to retail investors. Under a new regulation, investors who aren’t classified as professional buyers can start buying Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH), and the Tether (CRYPTO:USDT) stablecoin from November 17. However, purchases through any one intermediary are capped at 300,000 local currency a year, roughly $3,662 at the November 8 exchange rate.
US-listed crypto stocks showed little reaction. A major trading partner fell 1.5% to $134.76 on November 6, while a regional rival dipped 0.3% to $128.93. Bitcoin trades at $75,662 and Ethereum at $2,226 today. So can a cap this small move either coin’s price?
The country set the rules, but brokers decide how much money flows in.
The regulation has been officially released, naming the three cryptocurrencies eligible for purchase, the start date, and the cap for each intermediary. All buyers will also need to pass a knowledge test before investing. Qualified investors, on the other hand, face no purchase limits.
While the rules are clear, how retail buyers will reach the market remains uncertain. In October, the central bank authorized the largest bank in the country to provide crypto exchange services. On November 2, a major city announced plans to start Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT trading on December 1, beginning with pilot trades. However, the country hasn’t disclosed how many brokers it will license at launch, nor has it shared a demand forecast.
Since the 300,000 local currency cap applies to each intermediary, a buyer with accounts at several brokers could buy more than the cap in a year. That makes the theoretical ceiling look large on paper. Even so, the knowledge test, a potentially long licensing process, and restrictions on moving coins to private wallets could significantly reduce actual demand.
Why the major trading partner and regional rival stock showed little response.
The major trading partner can’t serve buyers from the country.
Because of OFAC sanctions, the major trading partner can’t serve customers from the country, so it won’t earn any direct revenue from the new regulation. Buying from the country could only help the major trading partner through higher crypto prices, which could in turn lift its trading and subscription income. Against the major trading partner’s third-quarter revenue of $1.22 billion, any such increase would be minimal. Our outlook looks at what moves the shares.
The regional rival’s value is tied to Bitcoin, not buyers from the country.
The regional rival holds about 848,517 BTC but has no retail customers. Executive Chairman told analysts on February 5 that crypto is moving from an asset class few could buy to one where everyone is competing to offer access. The country’s new rules support that view, but the regional rival’s stock closely follows Bitcoin’s price. Given that the cap applies inside a sanctioned country, the rule is unlikely to meaningfully move Bitcoin’s market value.
Earlier access milestones didn’t move prices much.
US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $1.28 billion in net outflows in the week to November 6. To offset that one week of outflows, about 350,000 buyers from the country would each need to buy the full annual cap.
History points the same way. When another country made Bitcoin legal tender on September 7, 2021, Bitcoin dropped that same day sharply. Similarly, the launch of another major city’s spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs in April 2024 didn’t lead to sustained price gains.
The country also plans to ban peer-to-peer crypto trading starting July 1, 2027. So some of the new regulated buying could come from existing traders in the country moving off informal channels ahead of that ban, rather than from new investors.
Will the 300,000 local currency cap move Bitcoin and Ethereum prices?
On the current evidence, the 300,000 local currency cap seems unlikely to move Bitcoin’s price much, and Ethereum looks even less likely to benefit. Bitcoin trades below its 20-day average of $79,362 and has slipped below its 30-day low close of $75,775, suggesting selling by US fund holders is a far bigger factor than potential buying from the country.
Ethereum also trades below its 30-day low close of $2,236, and capped buyers from the country might prefer Bitcoin, the better-known coin. If Bitcoin fails to reclaim its $79,362 20-day average before the major city’s December 1 launch, that would suggest the new rules had little effect on its price. For Ethereum, the key level is its $2,156 200-day average, about 3% below its price. Our look at Ethereum’s year-end outlook runs the longer numbers.
Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections.

full_texts.title: Major city faces power, heat and water outages after forces launch 36 missiles and 172 drones
full_texts.text:
The Briefing:
- Forces launched 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones at the capital and 12 other regions overnight on November 7 — only four missiles were intercepted, which the head of government blamed on critically depleted interceptor supplies.
- Several missiles struck the Northern Bridge over a major river, forcing a full closure; transmission facilities carrying electricity from two nuclear plants were also knocked offline, leaving the capital without power, heat, or water.
- The assault came three days before U.S.-brokered trilateral peace talks between a major city, the country, and the [another country] scheduled for November 10–11 in Abu Dhabi — an act the head of government described as deliberate intimidation ahead of negotiations.

Forces launched a massive overnight assault on the capital and surrounding areas on November 7, targeting energy infrastructure and a key crossing over the major river as temperatures in the capital hovered near freezing. The strike left the city struggling with electricity, water, and heating outages just days before a new round of U.S.-mediated peace negotiations.

Three Waves, Thirty-Six Missiles
The Air Force reported that forces deployed three successive waves of ballistic missiles alongside a large-scale drone barrage, striking the capital and 12 other regions simultaneously. All 36 ballistic missiles were directed at the capital and its surrounding area, the head of government said.
Of those 36 projectiles, air defenses brought down only four — a failure rate the head of government attributed directly to critically low interceptor reserves. Air defense units separately shot down 149 of the 172 drones deployed in the assault. Preliminary wreckage analysis at impact sites identified several of the missiles that penetrated defenses as North Korean-made KN-23 projectiles, a short-range ballistic weapon that has been supplied to a major power since late 2023.

Mayor confirmed that several missiles struck and damaged the Northern Bridge — one of the capital's primary arteries over the major river — severing trolleybus connections, damaging road surfaces, and cutting power lines. The crossing was closed in both directions as engineers assessed the structural damage.

Energy Grid Crippled as Winter Sets In
The overnight strikes concentrated on energy facilities across at least three districts of the capital region, with particular damage to the transmission infrastructure that channels electricity from two nuclear power plants into the capital and central regions. The Ministry of Energy described the results as severe.
"The capital is facing serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heating supplies," the head of government wrote on X, adding that substations in five other regions had also been knocked offline. With temperatures falling toward zero, municipal authorities warned residents to prepare for prolonged blackouts and disruptions to district heating networks. According to military intelligence, the major power held a stockpile of up to 700 ballistic missiles as of October 2026, with domestic production running at roughly 65 units per month.

At Least Two Dead, Damage Across Multiple Cities
At least two people were killed and injuries were reported across the country during the overnight strikes, according to authorities. Residential buildings, commercial properties, and non-residential structures sustained damage. In one neighborhood of the capital, residents searched through rubble and helped unearth a vehicle buried beneath earth displaced by a nearby missile impact.

A Calculated Message Three Days Before Abu Dhabi
The timing of the assault was widely read as a deliberate political statement. The attack landed just three days before a new round of trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi, where delegations from a major city and the country — with the [another country] acting as mediator — are scheduled to meet on November 10–11, as part of a U.S.-backed peace push that has so far produced few concrete results.
The head of government was unambiguous about the major power's intent. "The country is preparing for trilateral talks by launching ballistic missiles at critical infrastructure," he said, framing the bombardment as calculated intimidation rather than a conventional military strike. The major power's Defense Ministry offered a competing account, claiming its forces had struck targets within the military-industrial sector alongside energy and transport infrastructure in and around the capital.

The country Looks to a Newly Democratic Congress
The strikes also follow the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats swept to control of both chambers of Congress — a result that generated cautious optimism in the capital about the prospect of stronger legislative backing against the major power's campaign. The head of government said the country expected American lawmakers to sharpen their focus on the conflict given the major power's accelerating pace of attacks.
The major power has significantly intensified its aerial campaign in recent months as its ground offensive across eastern regions has largely stalled. Beyond targeting power grids, the major power has in recent weeks systematically struck the capital's crossings over the major river, disrupting the daily movement of more than three million people and steadily dismantling the infrastructure on which urban life depends as the country heads into the depths of winter.

full_texts.title: ‘We are a threat to the leader’: the small European news outlet with half its staff on the wanted list
full_texts.text:
The official newspaper of the government is an unlikely source of recognition for a European news outlet critical of the head of government and providing sanctuary to exiled journalists. But in May, two days after the country tested its new intercontinental ballistic missile system nicknamed "Satan II" by a major power, an article in the official newspaper prompted celebrations in a remote newsroom in the Arctic.
The story about how "leading global media" reacted to the missile test referred to just a handful of outlets including the BBC, Reuters, the Associated Press and [another country] 24. But among them was a small, journalist-owned online newspaper publishing in English and another language about northern regions and the Euro-Arctic region from a modest office in a major city.
It was especially surprising given that the publication had been declared an "undesirable organisation" by the office of the prosecutor general, and half of its staff journalists are on the wanted list.
Its editor said: "We were listed among what the government newspaper itself called ‘leading global media’. That was a very good day at the newspaper, because it means we had reached into the inner circle of the government."
Last week the head of government of a neighbouring country and the president of another neighbouring country held a call with the head of government, marking a rare moment of contact between the president and European leaders. Afterwards, the head of government said there were "big differences in views" with the president.
This certainly applies when it comes to press freedom. A few days later, the Nobel prize-winning independent newspaper was forced to close, citing intolerable pressure from authorities.
A short drive from the border and the only remaining legal land border crossing from the country into the European Schengen free travel area, the major city is a place where rising tensions with the capital are felt acutely. But since the full-scale invasion of a neighbouring country, the town has also become a refuge for individuals who have found themselves targeted by the regime – some of whom are journalists who have been hired by the newspaper.
Recently, a journalist, originally from a city in the country, appeared in the interior ministry’s database, accused of involvement with an “undesirable” organisation and failing to comply with the legal requirements for “foreign agents”. Officials in the city have filed a motion to detain the journalist in absentia.
He is the third journalist living in exile in the major city to be added to the wanted list. Despite this, like the rest of his colleagues he remains determined to continue his work unaffected.
"I can’t say this came as a surprise, given that the actions of the state are quite predictable and the initiation of criminal cases was only a matter of time," he said in an interview. "I don’t intend to change anything in my life because of this. Besides, they could have found me without declaring me wanted."
The journalist’s entry on to the wanted list came after his colleague was sentenced in absentia in July to six years in a penal colony on charges of “justifying terrorism” and “discrediting” the army.
Last year, the paper’s news editor was sentenced in absentia to eight years in prison for “spreading false information” about the army and “justifying terrorism”. She had previously been labelled a “foreign agent” and an unsuccessful extradition request was made to another country where she was living at the time.
Another journalist has also been added to the “foreign agents” registry, criminally charged and fined.
In the newspaper’s office, staff try to make light of the threats and intimidation by making a “wanted” wall with pictures from their wanted listings. While they have been living and working with pressure from across the border for years, the editor said there had been a “dramatic escalation” in the last few months.
"We are living very close to the border, so we probably saw things earlier than the rest of Europe," he said. But as a journalist, what concerns him most is the way the president is trying to assert media control beyond his own borders by targeting publications and exiled journalists in Europe.
Often when people are targeted by authorities, he said, they remove their names from public view and stop criticising the war on social media.
At the newspaper, they try to react by doing the opposite. "We maintain that the president is not a threat to us, we are a threat to him. Free and independent journalism is a threat to any dictatorship," the editor said.
Since being labelled a criminal organisation, making it a crime for people in the country to speak with its journalists, the newspaper has had to work even harder to get around the restrictions on its reporting. Its journalists do so using open sources, talking to people who are crossing the border, using satellite images, monitoring flight and shipping radars and speaking to exiled individuals. "I don’t want to say that this is easy. It’s getting harder and harder every day. But still possible," the editor said.
But they now face legal action in the high court in London from a billionaire, which they fear could bankrupt the newspaper. The complaint centres on five news stories published between 2025 and 2026 about a company that the billionaire co-founded and of which he is the majority owner.
One journalist was a 19-year-old student when she escaped house arrest by cutting off her electronic ankle bracelet and fleeing via another neighbouring country. A criminal case was opened against her after she reposted a message online about an explosion and was openly critical of the war.
When she first spoke to a major news outlet at the newspaper’s office in the major city in 2023, she had recently been hired as a journalist there. She arrived suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. "I was really afraid to be detained, captured, somehow sent back," she said.
Now, despite her recent sentencing, she speaks with cool pragmatism. "It doesn’t matter actually for special services where you are.
